newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: In Saddam's shadow, OPEC freezes.
newsitem.headline: In Saddam's shadow, OPEC freezes.

text.p: If any OPEC member harboured hopes of increasing oil output at ministerial talks this week to take advantage of a high price and buoyant demand, Saddam Hussein quickly dashed them.

Once again, the Iraqi strongman showed he has more influence right now on oil prices than all 10 other members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries put together, even though Baghdad has not sold a barrel since it invaded fellow OPEC member Kuwait more than six years ago.

News this week that a much-delayed United Nations plan to let Iraq sell some oil was back on track left the cartel no choice but to agree on Thursday to a new freeze on daily output at 25.03 million barrels until mid-1997.

"The issue of Iraq's return eclipsed the OPEC meeting entirely. All attention now shifts on winter demand and whether there will be any more obstacles to the Iraqi oil sale," said Michael Rothman, senior energy futures analyst at Merrill Lynch and Co in New York.
Though an output freeze had been widely expected by oil traders, there was speculation that higher prices would encourage some members to seek bigger quotas.

Sparked by Middle East tensions and increased pre-winter demand, prices in mid-October hit their highest since early 1991. Though the rally has cooled since then, world benchmark Brent Blend on Thursday was at $22.60 a barrel, up nearly $5 since OPEC last met in June.
OPEC members stand to reap an additional $30 billion this year in oil revenue, analysts say.

The timing of Iraq's return will be crucial to future price movement, analysts say. The head of Iraq's OPEC delegation, Osama al-Hiti, said on Wednesday he expected to be selling oil in "a matter of weeks."
Analysts say that if Iraqi barrels hit the market in the first six months of 1997, they should not make a big dent on prices.

"It looks like Iraqi oil will be coming back at the best possible time when demand is highest. The market needs that Iraqi oil right now," said Oysten Berentsen, head of crude trading at Statoil, the state oil company of Norway, OPEC's most formidable rival seller.

A Security Council sanctions committee on Wednesday approved a pricing formula, removing one of the last hurdles to implementing an Iraqi oil-for-food deal which could send between 500,000 to 600,000 barrels daily of Iraq's oil to the market in a matter of weeks.
On the surface. OPEC ministers seemed to take the news well, saying they had done enough to make room for Iraq when in June they increased its quota by 700,000 barrels daily to 1.2 million.

OPEC heavyweight Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, expects daily demand for OPEC oil to average 26.3 million in 1997, not far from current output of about 26 million even before Iraqi oil returns to the market.
Analysts also see no reason for a price collapse. They cite very low oil stocks and record high demand even before peak winter fuel use kicks in.

The OPEC of the 1990s, led by the Saudis, is more pragmatic than political. Today's OPEC is more likely to pore over spread sheets and supply-demand forecasts when determining production limits. It has not raised individual quotas except for Iraq since September 1993.

But most of the sacrifice has been made by Saudi Arabia and its Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates who have sat on mothballed capacity while the rest of OPEC and sellers outside the cartel have been pumping as much oil as they can.
"OPEC is more in tune with the market these days. Those with excess capacity are looking to maximize revenue through higher prices not volume," Statoil's Berentsen said.
Saudi minister Ali bin Ibrahim al-Nuaimi spoke of "market-determined activity" when asked how room would be made for Iraqi oil.
